Eddie Shore was a Canadian defenseman and one of hockey's earliest superstars, dominating the sport from the nineteen twenties through the nineteen forties. His physical, aggressive play and legendary toughness made him the standard-bearer for defenseman excellence in the era before Bobby Orr revolutionized the position.

Shore won the Hart Trophy for MVP four times in nineteen thirty-three, nineteen thirty-five, nineteen thirty-six, and nineteen thirty-eight, the most by any defenseman and a record that stood for decades. He played the majority of his career with the Boston Bruins from nineteen twenty-six to nineteen forty, establishing the franchise as a championship team during the original six-team era. He won the Stanley Cup twice with Boston in nineteen twenty-nine and nineteen thirty-nine, pioneering the Bruins' dynasty during hockey's early professional era.

Shore was known for his ferocious physical play, frequent fights, and willingness to dominate opponents through intimidation. He wore number two and accumulated scars that became legendary. He suffered multiple serious injuries including a fractured jaw, several concussions, and a separated shoulder, yet he returned repeatedly to dominate play. He was an exceptional skater for his era, combining speed with power, and revolutionized defensive play through aggressive checking and puck rushing. Later in life, he managed and coached, founding the Springfield Indians in the American Hockey League and serving as their owner.
